questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: That it was an english speaking country, that the university seemed decent in terms of academic performance and that the destination city was interesting.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was a bit disappointed in some of my units, but positively surprised on others.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I remember it being fairly easy. The headline for the arrival was information overload. A lot of the info was given several times, and you could have skipped the introduction week as much (if not all) of the information given here was repeated at the information events in th actual starting week.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I did not need assistance, as my units had been confirmed by USYD before arrival.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Only complaint would be information overload. This was most likely because the university engages in so many aspects of the student's life, meaning you received information not only about things related directly to studying at the university, but also about water safety, housing, scamming (housing, telephone, e-mail), food services, social clubs and events, police, medical service and more.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
The housing market for international students seems to be dominated by landlords / professional housing managers who owns houses/apartments and rent individual rooms out to students and workers. The quality of these houses are low and the prices are high. As an european exchange student it is easy to get your hands on an expensive room, but you will have a harder time finding shared accommodation with people who are themselves looking to live socially with other people.

Friends of mine who lived on campus were disappointed with the cleaning standard of the common kitchen, but their rooms and other facilities were definitely of higher quality (and price).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: The prices are in general higher than Copenhagen while the quality is lower. It is normal to have inspection of the room (usually a whole group of interested tenants comes to see the room at once), so you can definitely wait to find a room until arrival, but it is a lottery in terms of how nice a place you can find.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The units they advertise online to be available to exchange students are not necessarily so. You have to mail the international student coordinator and ask for a list (google sheet) of the available units. I believe the number of actual available units is smaller than what is advertised through their online catalogue.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You sign up through an online portal and then you later receive notice whether you have been assigned to the unit. You should list more units than desired, as you might not be assigned and/or approved to all. I was not approved for two units, as I did not meet the requirements (I had not send anything forward, which is a possibility), but I was allowed to do one of them anyway (I don't know why).

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can mail with the international student coordinator. She was super busy, and would take a week or so to reply.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I wanted classes that were advertised to be open for exchange students in their online catalogue, but this was apparently a mistake. In the end I got four units I wanted, where two of them were units I choose because I could not get any other units within my main field of interest.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Do not choose this university because of the units before you have looked at the actual list of units available for you. For this, you have to mail the student coordinator and ask for the list.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: In genereal, the level of the units seemed lower than at UCPH. The students seem to have less experience with academic writing. I was pretty challenged in one class, but this class was also outside of my faculty (I am political science student and the class was as their computer science faculty).

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I find the instructors/teachers teaching the discussion classes better at UCPH. In some units, the classes were pretty much an extra mini lecture (in a bad way).

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Chinese Politics
Issues in Public Policy 
Principles of Data Science 
Visual Data Analytics

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
If you already have some experience with machine learning, then you might be disappointed with Principles of Data Science. In the beginning it was way to easy (I believe to introduce people with no former experience to quantitative methods to the subject), and then later you will work a new algorithm or approach every week. This was fine, but because the unit is pretty demanding in terms of assignments during the unit, I found myself not focusing enough of on the weekly material (where I would have gained more relevant knowledge) and too much on the group assignments.

If you are looking for a very easy low demanding unit, Visual Data Analytics is a good choice.

Chinese Politics was interesting and the teacher good, and you do not need to know much of this area beforehand. 

Issues in Public Policy was difficult when you do not know a lot about Australian politics and history, but nonetheless an interesting look into this and also cases broader than just Australia. This unit was very much case driven.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Food (grocery shopping) and gym was super expensive.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Eating out and public transport was a bit cheaper than expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Many clubs and social events all the time.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Everything you can think of... Many sports you could do on campus: climbing/bouldering, football, swimming, archery, volleyball, fitness, fitness classes, self defense. Many social, academic, religious clubs as well.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: For free you can attend a spors tournament between faculties, each week a new sport. You sign up though you faculty's facebook page.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Many things going on the city you can do like concerts, sport events and such. Also enjoy the nature and beaches.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy. Most students on master level are international students. In general, it is easy to find friends and people to talk to. More difficult to find deeper connections, which I found more difficult to establish with non-scandinavians. I think this is a cultural difference.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Attend social events or even just chat up someone around campus. People are very openminded like that. I found made a friend just by sitting next to him in the library.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The greeting of "how are you" lol. You are not supposed to actually answer, I ended up just trying to say it before the other person.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Openness and outdoor.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Get your hands on the (secret) list of actual availlable units before deciding on this uni.
2. Prepare yourself for debt (SU-loan, maybe) unless you have a good savings account
3. Research areas to live in and the whole housing situation

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
One heads up might be group work. Almost all exchange students I knew endured som bad experiences, where group members would slack and not contribute. I believe this is due to the workload in terms of assignments during the semester and the pressure some students feel for obtaining good grades. I had two groups, one which was great (apart from a non-trivial language barrier (they were Chinese), and another with was the worst group experience I ever had. Therefore, be aware of this issue early in a project, so you can address the situation accordingly.

Also, if you take classes at the Business School and Computer Science, you might experience to be the only non-Chinese student in your class. This is because very few Australians get a master and Australia receives many Asian and specifically Chinese international students.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Living a new place and gaining new friends and experiences. Not having all the commitments as back home gave a lot freedom.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Striking the right balance between studying and having a good time.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
